walkthroughs.body_html:
The Challenge of Resource Management — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Challenge of Resource Management brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Challenge of Resource Management.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the Hubbert curve about?
options: Peak oil
Population
Climate
Migration
Africa
South America
Australia
Central Asia

mcqs.q: Is water scarcity in a country always due to low rainfall?
options: Water scarcity happens when reservoirs are painted dark colours.
Only dry countries face water insecurity.
No — economic scarcity occurs where rainfall is adequate but storage, treatment and distribution infrastructure are lacking; physical scarcity is about the supply itself.
Imported food contains no calories.

mcqs.q: Does importing much of its food mean the UK has no food security?
options: Not necessarily — diverse import sources spread risk and the UK still produces a substantial share of its food, though import reliance does raise exposure to price shocks and supply disruption.
Imported food contains no calories.
Food imports mean a country has zero food security.
Energy security means guarding power stations with fences.

mcqs.q: Is energy security only about how much energy a country produces?
options: Energy security means guarding power stations with fences.
No — it also involves affordability, reliability of imports, diversity of the energy mix and managing demand; a big producer can still be insecure if supply is undiversified.
Producing lots of energy automatically makes a country energy secure.
Water scarcity happens when reservoirs are painted dark colours.
